Drink water through the day. Don't wait until you feel thirsty.
Try to go to bed and wake up at the same time every day. It helps you sleep better.
Put your phone away 30 to 60 minutes before bed. It helps you fall asleep more easily.
Caffeine can keep you awake for hours. Try to avoid coffee, tea, and energy drinks in the afternoon and evening.
Try to move your body a little every day. A 30-minute walk on most days is a great start.
If you sit a lot, stand up and stretch every hour.
A few gentle stretches after exercise can help your muscles feel less tight.
Take the stairs when you can. Small moves add up.
Try to eat fruits and vegetables of different colors. Each color gives your body different good things.
Whole grains, beans, fruit, and vegetables help your stomach work well and keep you full for longer.
Sugary drinks have a lot of sugar. Try swapping one a day for water.
Too much salt can raise your blood pressure. Check food labels and pick lower-salt options.
Keep healthy snacks like fruit or nuts nearby so it's easier to snack well.
Feeling stressed? Breathe in slowly, then out even slower, for one or two minutes.
Talking to a friend, a family member, or a doctor about how you feel can make stress feel lighter.
Spend 10 to 20 minutes outside in daylight. It can lift your mood and help you sleep.
Before bed, think of three good things that happened today.
Wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds, especially before eating and after using the toilet.
Brush your teeth twice a day for two minutes, and clean between your teeth once a day.
Wear sunscreen and a hat when you are outside, and put on more sunscreen every two hours.
Tired eyes from screens? Every 20 minutes, look at something far away for 20 seconds.
Keep your screen at eye level and your feet flat on the floor. It is easier on your neck and back.
If you can't hear the people around you when you wear headphones, the volume is too loud.
Go to regular check-ups, even when you feel fine. Problems are easier to treat when they are found early.
Keep medicines in a cool, dry place away from sunlight. Bathrooms are often too humid.
Check the expiry dates on your medicines often. Take expired ones to a pharmacy to throw away safely.
Keep medicines in their original box or bottle so you always know the name, instructions, and expiry date.
Never take someone else's prescription medicine or give yours to someone else. What is safe for one person can be harmful to another.
Tell your doctor or pharmacist about everything you take, including vitamins and herbal products. Some don't mix well.
Keep a list of your medicines on your phone so you can show it to a doctor quickly.
Set a phone alarm or use a pill box to help you remember to take your medicine.
Use the small cup or syringe that comes with liquid medicine. A kitchen spoon can give the wrong amount.
Many cold and flu medicines contain the same ingredient. Read the labels so you don't take too much by accident.
Don't crush or cut tablets unless your pharmacist says it's okay. Some are made to release slowly.
Take antibiotics exactly how your doctor tells you. Don't save leftovers for next time.
Some medicines don't mix with certain foods or drinks, like grapefruit or alcohol. Ask your pharmacist.
If you miss a dose, read the leaflet or ask your pharmacist what to do. Don't take a double dose unless they tell you to.
Keep all medicines up high, out of children's sight and reach.
Don't throw old medicines in the trash or flush them. Take them to a pharmacy.
Paracetamol (also called acetaminophen) helps with pain and fever. Never take more than the amount on the label, because too much can hurt your liver.
Ibuprofen helps with pain, fever, and swelling. Take it with food to protect your stomach. Ask a pharmacist first if you have stomach, kidney, or heart problems.
Aspirin helps with pain and fever. Don't give it to children or teenagers who have a cold or the flu.
Naproxen is a pain and swelling medicine that lasts longer than ibuprofen. Take it with food.
Amoxicillin is an antibiotic for infections caused by bacteria. It does not work on colds or the flu. Tell your doctor if you are allergic to penicillin.
Azithromycin is an antibiotic that is often taken for just a few days. Take it exactly as your doctor says.
Omeprazole lowers stomach acid and helps with heartburn. It is usually taken before a meal.
Antacids give quick relief from heartburn. They can affect other medicines, so ask your pharmacist how far apart to take them.
Loperamide helps stop diarrhea. See a doctor if you also have a high fever or blood in your stool.
Oral rehydration salts replace the water and salts your body loses with diarrhea or vomiting. They are especially helpful for children and older adults.
Loratadine is an allergy medicine that helps with sneezing and itchy eyes. It usually does not make you sleepy.
Cetirizine is an allergy medicine for sneezing and itching. It can make some people sleepy, so be careful when driving.
Diphenhydramine is an allergy medicine that often makes you sleepy. Don't drive after taking it.
Salbutamol (also called albuterol) is a "reliever" inhaler for asthma that opens the airways fast. If you need it more and more often, talk to your doctor.
Metformin is a common medicine for type 2 diabetes. It helps your body control blood sugar. Taking it with food can help avoid an upset stomach.
Insulin is used to control blood sugar in diabetes. Unopened insulin is usually kept in the fridge, and the injection spot should be changed each time.
Amlodipine is a medicine for high blood pressure. Swollen ankles can be a side effect, so tell your doctor if you notice it.
Lisinopril is a medicine for high blood pressure. Some people get a dry cough from it.
Atorvastatin lowers cholesterol. Tell your doctor if you get muscle pain you can't explain, and ask your pharmacist about grapefruit.
Warfarin is a blood thinner. It mixes badly with many foods and medicines, so you need regular blood tests. Try to eat about the same amount of green leafy vegetables each week.
Levothyroxine replaces thyroid hormone. It works best when taken on an empty stomach at the same time every day.
Hydrocortisone cream helps with itchy skin and rashes. Use a thin layer for a short time, and don't use it on your face unless a doctor says so.
Vitamin D keeps your bones and muscles strong. You get it from sunlight, some foods, and supplements. Ask a doctor before taking high doses.
Iron supplements help when your iron is low. They can cause constipation and dark stools. Keep them away from children, because too many can be very dangerous.
Folic acid is a vitamin that is especially important before and during early pregnancy for the baby's development.
Melatonin is a supplement some people use to change their sleep time, like with jet lag. It is best for short-term use, after talking to a doctor.
Vitamin B12 helps your nerves and blood. People who eat little meat, eggs, or dairy, or who have stomach problems, may need a supplement.
Saline nasal spray is a salt-water spray that helps clear a blocked nose. It is safe for most people to use often.
Throat lozenges can ease a sore throat. Check the label, because some contain medicine that can add up with other products you take.
Artificial tears are eye drops for dry, tired eyes. Wash your hands first, and don't let the bottle tip touch your eye.
